newsitem.title: USA: U.S. finds little support for joint action on Cuba.
newsitem.headline: U.S. finds little support for joint action on Cuba.

text.p: U.S. envoy Stuart Eizenstat said on Friday he failed in a first round of visits to win support from U.S. allies for a multi-nation effort to press for democracy in Cuba.

Eizenstat, the commerce undersecretary for international trade, said his tour of Canada, Mexico, Belgium and Ireland was "a lightning rod" for criticism of the Helms-Burton law, which restricts trade with Cuba. He planned visits to Spain, Germany and Britain next week.
"At the government level, quite frankly, it was quite difficult to get them to work through their anger at the Helms-Burton act," Eizenstat told reporters.
He said "it's going to be some period of time" before any consensus might emerge for joint action. He said he would make additional trips over the next few months.

President Bill Clinton has said international cooperation on Cuba will be a factor in deciding whether to again suspend in January a Helms-Burton provision that allows lawsuits against foreign firms who profit from property confiscated from U.S. citizens after the 1959 Cuban revolution.

During a telephone news conference, Eizenstat said the United States was committed to multilateral trade rules, despite criticism that Helms-Burton marked a trend toward unilateral action. Mexico, Canada and the European Union have strongly criticized the law.
A number of nations have begun preparing "antidote" laws to override the U.S. law.

The United States would stoutly defend Helms-Burton if it was challenged in the World Trade Organization or under the North American Free Trade Agreement, he said. A challenge would only raise trade tensions and be in no one's interest.

In addition to the provisions allowing lawsuits, the Helms-Burton law codified the U.S. economic embargo, would allow the embargo to be lifted only when a democratic government was installed and allowed the United States to bar entry of foreign nationals who are found to be "trafficking" in property confiscated from U.S. citizens.
In early July, the Clinton administration said it would bar seven executives and board members from Sheritt International Corp, a Canadian mining firm, from the United States.

The State Department said on August 19 that "a number of executives" -- fewer than 10 -- from Mexican telecommunications company Grupo Domos would be barred unless the firm amended its operations during a 45-day grace period.
Eizenstat said he told allies that Helms-Burton had a much tighter focus than was feared. He said a dozen firms were under investigation for possible violations.
